summary:
Visitors to Bauchi State stand under two overlapping criminal regimes. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public displays of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and Human Rights Watch has documented police using it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. On top of that, Bauchi's Sharia Penal Code remains in force: the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms the religious penal codes of all twelve northern Nigerian states, Bauchi among them, and records male sodomy as carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Bauchi is the one state where that capital ceiling has actually been pronounced for same-sex conduct. On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men, one of them 70-year-old Malam Haruna, to death by stoning for homosexuality under Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard, who told the court the three were arrested at Gwada village on 14 June 2022. Reuters reported the case on 2 July 2022 as the first time the death penalty had been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. Presiding judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi granted a 30-day appeal window, and relatives told Punch in July 2022 that the sentence had not been carried out at that point. The UK Home Office note adds that a stoning sentence cannot be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and records a further death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Bauchi Sharia court in May 2024.

Capital sentences for sodomy in Bauchi have a history of being overturned on appeal. Amnesty International's 2004 press release records that the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's death-by-stoning sentence, handed down on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, on grounds of denial of counsel and a defective confession, following the quashing of Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction on 14 November 2003. Amnesty described a pattern of convictions and death sentences quashed on appeal.

Vigilante pressure accompanies the courts. In January 2014 an angry mob stormed Bauchi's Tudun Alkali Upper Sharia Court during a sodomy trial demanding a death sentence, as recorded by the UK Home Office.

Gender expression itself is a charged offence in Bauchi. State police arrested eighteen men and charged them with sodomy for dressing as women under the Sharia penal code; the charges were later reduced to vagrancy and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial, with the pre-trial detention dissolving by the end of 2011. Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held under Sharia charges for years.

No source records where such detainees are housed inside custody, whether in a male or female wing, a special unit, or solitary confinement, and no trans-specific placement rule, facility or policy is documented for Bauchi. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Bauchi's record sits within a national pattern of weaponised enforcement. The Thomson Reuters Foundation documented in April 2024 kito gangs who lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, a risk that applies to visitors using dating apps anywhere in Nigeria.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement nationwide. In March 2025 TimesLIVE reported that Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months later no suspects had been charged, according to the Dial's February 2025 account.

Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here; Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians lived in fear of such proposals.
